summary:
We developed MODIIRS, a web application that harmonizes MODIS and VIIRS fire hot spots from NASA FIRMS into a single burn activity calendar for 2000–2026. For any area a user draws in Mexico, it shows whether this month's fire activity is normal or anomalous against that area's own history.

It addresses the challenge by removing sensor bias. MODIS (1 km pixels) and VIIRS (375 m pixels) cannot simply be added: when VIIRS arrived in 2012, raw counts in central Mexico's Bajío jumped 14.7 times with no real change in fire. We count cell-days (places and days with fire, not points) and convert VIIRS to MODIS-equivalent units with a factor k measured where both sensors overlapped. The false jump drops to 1.07 times.

This matters because MODIS on Terra and Aqua is near retirement. Without harmonization, fire managers lose their 26-year baseline. With it, the record continues on VIIRS alone, with its error measured and shown.
details:
WHAT DOES IT DO AND HOW DOES IT WORK?

MODIIRS is a burn activity calendar for any area of interest in Mexico, from 2000 to 2026. The user picks an example region, draws a rectangle or polygon, or types coordinates. The app shows a year-by-month calendar, the fire of the selected month on a 3D map, a card for each hot spot (satellite, date, radiative power), and CSV downloads of the calendar and the hot spots.

The method has four steps:

1. Filter non-vegetation sources. Cells classified by FIRMS as a static source (type = 2) on three or more dates are masked: they are industry, not fire. Sensor outages are detected per satellite, and affected months are flagged.

2. Count places, not points. The unit is the cell-day: a 0.01° × 0.01° cell (about 1 km) with at least one vegetation fire detection on a given day. Ten VIIRS points on one fire count once, so a finer sensor cannot inflate the record. Only one reference VIIRS is used per day (S-NPP before April 2018, NOAA-20 after), so three satellites in orbit do not triple the count.

3. Calibrate where both sensors overlap. Over the 167 months when MODIS and VIIRS operated together (February 2012 to December 2025), k = MODIS cell-days / VIIRS cell-days, computed for the exact area the user selected. Then MODIS_eq = k × VIIRS. The factor is validated by leaving one year out at a time (LOYO): k is recomputed without that year and used to predict it. A monthly error (MAPE) is reported as well.

4. Classify each month against its own history. Each month is compared with the median and percentiles (p25, p75, p90) of the same calendar month in the other years, with at least 10 years required. The result is a level: Low, Normal, High or Extreme. Months with a MODIS or VIIRS outage, partial months and months without files are excluded from the baseline. "No data" is never shown as zero.

WHAT BENEFITS DOES IT HAVE AND WHAT IS THE INTENDED IMPACT?

Fire managers, civil protection agencies, protected-area staff and researchers get one comparable 26-year record for their own area, plus an honest measure of its uncertainty.

Measured results on the full Mexico database (9.5 million detections):

- The false jump disappears. Raw points from 2011 to 2019 rise 14.7 times in the Querétaro Bajío, 12.4 times in Sierra Gorda and 13.9 times in the full Querétaro box. Harmonized cell-days change by 1.07, 0.92 and 1.01 times.

- The factor is regional, not global. k = 0.260 in Sierra Gorda, 0.304 in the Bajío and 0.290 in the full Querétaro box; across other places tested in Mexico it ranges from 0.24 to 0.69. An early measurement on Chilecito, Argentina (the challenge's reference fire) gave k = 0.40. This is why the app computes k for each area instead of using one fixed number.

- The error is known. Leave-one-year-out annual error is 5.9 % (Querétaro box), 10.1 % (Bajío) and 17.2 % (Sierra Gorda). The error for a single month is 33–37 %, so the app reports levels by percentile rather than promising exact monthly figures.

- It finds real signals. February 2026 is the most active month in 26 years in the Bajío: 150 cell-days, 5 times the median.

- The record survives MODIS. With "Simulate the end of MODIS", the series uses VIIRS × k from 2012 on. In the Bajío the annual total changes 9 % (median) and the monthly level stays the same or one step away in 89 % of months.

- It is fast. The calendar for a newly drawn area returns in about 0.2 seconds.

The MVP covers Mexico. Argentina is already loaded in the database for the next phase, and the formulas do not change by country.

Declared limits: a cloudy month can look like a quiet month; the tool does not predict fires or measure burned area; it compares each month with its own history.

WHAT TOOLS, CODING LANGUAGES, HARDWARE OR SOFTWARE DID YOU USE?

- Data processing: Python 3.12, Polars, psycopg (COPY), SQL.

- Database: PostgreSQL 16 + PostGIS, in a podman container.

- API: FastAPI, Pydantic, Shapely, Uvicorn.

- Frontend: React, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind CSS, MapLibre GL (WebGL, 3D terrain).

- Map data: OpenFreeMap vector tiles and Mapzen Terrarium elevation tiles.

- Hardware: a single laptop. No cloud services.

HOW IS YOUR PROJECT CREATIVE?

- The cell-day. Instead of correcting point counts, we changed the unit: we count where and on how many days there was fire.

- A factor measured for the user's own area, with its validation shown next to it in a "k-factor inspector".

- "Simulate the end of MODIS": one switch rebuilds 14 years of history without MODIS, live, so anyone can see what the record will look like after the sensor retires.

- A time console styled like a satellite operations screen: the 2000–2026 timeline has one track per sensor, and the lit part shows which sensor feeds the series each month.

- A Learn view, "Don Modesto's notebook", that walks through the method in four steps with real data and a short quiz.

- Zero and "no data" look different on purpose: zero is a dark tile, "no data" is a hatched tile.

WHAT FACTORS SUCH AS ENERGY, ACCESSIBILITY OR COST DID YOUR TEAM CONSIDER?

- Accessibility: three palettes (thermal, colorblind-safe blue–yellow, high contrast); the level is always written in words and marked with a symbol, not only colored; optional sonification with the Web Audio API (one tone per level); full keyboard navigation; support for the system's reduced-motion setting; Spanish and English.

- Energy: the map repaints only when something changes; animations use transform and opacity only; the views that are not open are not downloaded; API responses are compressed (about 6.5 KB per calendar) and cached in memory.

- Cost: only open data and open-source software. Open map tiles with no paid API keys. Everything runs on one laptop.
